name: Peptide YY

lead: Peptide YY is a 36-amino-acid hormone released by cells in the ileum and colon after you eat, signalling fullness. A 2002 Nature report that PYY(3-36) injection reduced food intake in rodents and human volunteers sparked interest in it for weight control.

The main circulating form, PYY(3-36), binds Y2 receptors, including on appetite-regulating neurons in the hypothalamus, and slows stomach emptying. The chain is a stronger fullness signal, lower intake, then fat loss and a leaner look. Levels rise with meals, especially protein-rich ones.

paras: People interested in appetite control discuss it mainly through protein-rich meals that raise natural PYY levels. Human research has used small infusion studies, and an oral/lingual delivery trial is registered. No PYY drug is approved for weight management.
Published material does not detail safety outcomes of PYY analogues. Research use is investigational and it has no regulatory approval for weight management.

angle.text: Peptide YY is a gut hormone that signals fullness after meals, so you eat less and lose fat toward a leaner look. Infusion studies showed reduced food intake. It is not an approved weight-loss drug.

lead: Peptide YY (PYY) is a 36-amino-acid gut hormone released by L-cells in the ileum and colon after eating. It acts to reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying, and it belongs to the neuropeptide Y family [1][2]. The main circulating form, PYY(3-36), acts largely through the Y2 receptor [3][2].

For appearance, the interest in PYY is a fat-loss chain: a meal-triggered fullness signal that lowers how much a person eats, which over time can reduce body fat and sharpen the face and physique. In 2002, researchers reported in Nature that peripheral injection of PYY(3-36) reduced food intake in rodents and in human volunteers, which led to interest in it as an anti-obesity agent [4]. It is not an approved drug for weight management or appearance. Research is investigational, with small human infusion studies and an oral/lingual delivery trial registered [2][5].

PYY is also part of the wider story of gut hormones that now underpins GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Reviews of appetite regulation group PYY with GLP-1, CCK and oxyntomodulin as hormones that dampen hunger after meals, while ghrelin pushes the other way [6][7]. Many people who talk about raising PYY in fitness and diet circles are in practice discussing protein-rich meals, fibre and sleep, which are reported to influence its release [2][8][9].
infobox: 36 amino acids; molecular weight about 4.3 kDa [3]
Research only; no approved PYY drug

paras: PYY is secreted after meals in proportion to calorie content, and levels fall during fasting [4][2]. The enzyme DPP-4 converts PYY(1-36) to PYY(3-36), the predominant circulating form, which is highly selective for the Y2 receptor [2][10]. Protein intake is reported to raise PYY levels [2]. PYY also slows gastric emptying and promotes water and electrolyte absorption in the colon [2].

Obese people have been reported to secrete less PYY after a meal, though some studies find they remain sensitive to its appetite-reducing effect, so reduced sensitivity is not considered established as a cause of obesity [2]. After bariatric surgery, gut hormone profiles, including PYY, shift toward an appetite-suppressing pattern [11]. A study of people on a diet-induced weight-loss programme reported long-lasting hormonal changes, including altered gut hormones, after weight loss [12].

PYY shares the characteristic folded structure of the neuropeptide Y family, in which a polyproline-type helix folds back onto an alpha helix, and it is amidated at its C-terminal end [3]. After release, the enzyme DPP-4 removes two amino acids from the N-terminus; this shifts the peptide from a broad-acting form that binds several NPY-family receptors to PYY(3-36), which is selective for Y2 [2][10]. Y2 receptors sit on arcuate-nucleus neurons that make neuropeptide Y, and the 2002 report proposed that PYY(3-36) acts there to inhibit those appetite-stimulating cells [4].

Besides appetite, PYY slows gastric emptying and intestinal transit, an effect sometimes called the ileal or colonic brake, and it promotes water and electrolyte absorption in the colon [2]. A 2023 Science paper reported a separate role for PYY as an antimicrobial peptide made by Paneth cells that helps maintain the gut yeast Candida as a commensal [13].

PYY release is reported to rise with meal size and with protein intake [4][2]. Short-chain fatty acids produced when gut bacteria ferment fibre, notably propionate, stimulated PYY and GLP-1 secretion through the free fatty acid receptor 2 in rodent experiments [14]. A review of sleep and circadian biology discusses PYY alongside ghrelin and leptin as one of the appetite hormones affected by insufficient sleep and circadian misalignment [8].
A network meta-analysis of single-dose trials examined how non-nutritive sweetened beverages affect postprandial glucose and endocrine responses compared with water and sugar-sweetened drinks [9].

Kazuhiko Tatemoto isolated PYY in 1982 from pig intestine as a candidate gut hormone, and the same laboratory described the sequence of neuropeptide Y, which proved structurally related [1][14][2]. Its distribution and release in humans were described in 1985 [15]. The nomenclature of the NPY, PYY and pancreatic polypeptide receptor family was formalised by an International Union of Pharmacology committee in 1998 [16].

A 2002 Nature paper by Batterham and colleagues reported that PYY(3-36) inhibited food intake [4], and a 2003 New England Journal of Medicine study reported that infusion cut calorie intake at a buffet meal by roughly 30% in obese and lean subjects [2]. Interest then widened to the other gut hormones, and the later arrival of GLP-1-based medicines made gut-brain satiety signalling one of the most active areas of obesity research [7][6].

Obese people have been reported to secrete less PYY after a meal, though some studies find they remain sensitive to its appetite-reducing effect, so reduced PYY sensitivity is not considered established as a cause of obesity [2]. After bariatric surgery, gut hormone profiles, including higher PYY, shift toward an appetite-suppressing pattern, and researchers have linked this to weight loss after the operations [11]. A study of people on a diet-induced weight-loss programme reported hormonal changes after weight loss, including altered gut hormones, that persisted over time and were proposed as a contributor to weight regain [12].
Reviews of the molecular basis of obesity list PYY(3-36) with leptin, insulin and ghrelin as signals that integrate with brain circuits controlling feeding [17].

Beyond injected PYY analogues, researchers have examined indirect approaches. A trial of targeted colonic delivery of propionate, a short-chain fatty acid, in overweight adults measured effects on PYY and GLP-1 release, appetite and weight gain [18]. Gut microbiota that ferment fibre are also discussed as influencing gut hormone secretion [10][19]. Gut hormones including PYY are covered among the incretin and related hormones in a 2018 review [20], and a 2024 review covers meal timing, food quality, exercise type and sleep deprivation as environmental factors that shape gut hormone responses [7].

Combination approaches are the direction of current drug development: the 2024 review notes that triple-agonist and partial-agonist drugs acting on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors have produced weight loss in trials, while PYY itself has not reached the market [7].

Human studies of PYY itself are small. Registered investigations include PYY infusion studies in obese adults (24 participants each) examining food intake [21], a phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic study of single intravenous doses in overweight adults (31 participants) [22], a study of PYY degradation in healthy volunteers [23], and a trial of lingual PYY(3-36) on appetite and energy intake, with unknown status [5]. A phase 1 dose-escalation safety study of a compound called GT-001 was also registered under feeding and eating disorders [24].

Published reports of infusion studies described reduced intake over a meal, as noted above [4][2]. The propionate trial found that colonic delivery was associated with increased PYY and GLP-1 and with less weight gain over 24 weeks in overweight adults [18]. A randomised controlled trial in females with lipedema compared gastrointestinal hormones and subjective appetite ratings after low-carbohydrate versus low-fat low-energy diets [25]. No PYY product is approved for weight loss.

Published material on PYY analogues describes research use only. Safety and tolerability of single intravenous doses was the subject of a phase 1 registration in overweight adults [22]. No regulatory agency has approved a PYY drug for weight management, and PYY is not sold as a medicine for appearance.
